newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Justice on trial in Belgian child sex scandal.
newsitem.headline: Justice on trial in Belgian child sex scandal.

text.p: Belgian justice went on trial on Tuesday as commentators reacted against a move by the lawyer defending chief child sex scandal suspect Marc Dutroux to get the investigating magistrate thrown off the case.

Lawyer Julien Pierre has formally asked for magistrate Jean-Marc Connerotte to be removed on the grounds of bias because he did not pay for a dinner he was invited to by a support group for the parents of missing and murdered children.

"This manoeuvre is simply a new example of justice being taken hostage by the misuse of the legal means put at the disposal of the defence," Jean-Pierre Malmendier of the Marc et Corinne support group, said. The group was named after two children who were abducted and killed in the late 1980s.
"Isn't it more important to establish the rights of the victims?" he asked Belgian media.

Malmendier accepted that Connerotte and public prosecutor Michel Bourlet had not paid for their pasta dinner on September 21, but he rejected claims by Pierre that they had contributed to a fund for the children.
Newspapers said there had been unprecedented public demonstrations in support of Connerotte and Bourlet -- an indication of the depth of feelings in the scandal.
Lawyer Pierre, who took the case after several others had turned it down, has received threatening telephone calls.

The unmasking of the child abduction, sexual abuse and murder ring allegedly led by convicted child rapist Dutroux has left Belgium in a state of shock and prompted hitherto unasked questions about the moral and political health of the country.

"The confidence of our citizens in our institutions has been shaken," Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene told the opening session of the new parliamentary year. "What we are experiencing today touches the very essence and the future of our society."
Four young girls have been found dead since mid-August -- two at least starved to death. Two others have been rescued.
Police have found the body of an accomplice whom Dutroux admits killing, and are searching for seven other children.
The case has revealed a catalogue of bungling, incompetence and rivalry between different police forces and the judiciary, and prompted allegations of possible police complicity.
The arrest late on Monday of gendarme Gerard Vannesse on charges of drug trafficking and car theft -- the other side of the Dutroux case -- will have done nothing to dispel the fears.
"It is truly a hurricane that has battered our country these past weeks," Dehaene said. "During the coming months the government will take important decisions on this matter,"

Dehaene said these key decisions would cover the appointment of public prosecutors, the division of responsibilities between different police forces, relations between the police and the judiciary and the enforcement of penalties.

Vannesse was the 13th person -- and the second police officer -- to be arrested and charged in the case. Seven people, including Dutroux, his second wife Michelle Martin and flamboyant businessman Jean-Michel Nihoul remain in detention.
Belgian newspapers reported that unemployed Dutroux had millions of francs stashed in bank accounts around the country.
The Cour de Cassation, Belgium's highest court, will have to decide whether to uphold Pierre's complaint against Connerotte.

But even if the court rejects the move, the early tabling of the motion against Connerotte leaves open the possibility of a later appeal to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, which could prolong the case for years.
That is an eventuality that few Belgians would relish -- uncomfortable as they already are in the glare of adverse international publicity created by the case.
